fetched_contents.text: COCO Dataset The COCO (Common Objects in Context) dataset is a large-scale object detection, segmentation, and captioning dataset. It is designed to encourage research on a wide variety of object categories and is commonly used for benchmarking computer vision models. It is an essential dataset for researchers and developers working on object detection, segmentation, and pose estimation tasks. Watch: Ultralytics COCO Dataset Overview COCO Pretrained Models Model size mAPval mAPval Speed Speed params FLOPs (pixels) 50-95 50-95(e2e) CPU ONNX T4 TensorRT10 (M) (B) (ms) (ms) YOLO26n 640 40.9 40.1 38.9 ± 0.7 1.7 ± 0.0 2.4 5.4 YOLO26s 640 48.6 47.8 87.2 ± 0.9 2.5 ± 0.0 9.5 20.7 YOLO26m 640 53.1 52.5 220.0 ± 1.4 4.7 ± 0.1 20.4 68.2 YOLO26l 640 55.0 54.4 286.2 ± 2.0 6.2 ± 0.2 24.8 86.4 YOLO26x 640 57.5 56.9 525.8 ± 4.0 11.8 ± 0.2 55.7 193.9 Key Features * COCO contains 330K images, with 200K images having annotations for object detection, segmentation, and captioning tasks. * The dataset comprises 80 object categories, including common objects like cars, bicycles, and animals, as well as more specific categories such as umbrellas, handbags, and sports equipment. * Annotations include object bounding boxes, segmentation masks, and captions for each image. * COCO provides standardized evaluation metrics like mean Average Precision (mAP) for object detection, and mean Average Recall (mAR) for segmentation tasks, making it suitable for comparing model performance. Dataset Structure The COCO dataset is split into three subsets: 1. Train2017: This subset contains 118K images for training object detection, segmentation, and captioning models. 2. Val2017: This subset has 5K images used for validation purposes during model training. 3. Test2017: This subset consists of 20K images used for testing and benchmarking the trained models. Ground truth annotations for this subset are not publicly available, and the results are submitted to the COCO evaluation server for performance evaluation. Applications The COCO dataset is widely used for training and evaluating deep learning models in object detection (such as Ultralytics YOLO, Faster R-CNN, and SSD), instance segmentation (such as Mask R-CNN), and keypoint detection (such as OpenPose). The dataset's diverse set of object categories, large number of annotated images, and standardized evaluation metrics make it an essential resource for computer vision researchers and practitioners. Mini-report on the dataset’s key features and structure

COCO is structured as a large-scale object detection, segmentation, and captioning dataset, with a design aimed at benchmarking computer vision models across multiple tasks [N1-F1]. Its dataset YAML shows that it contains 330K images, with 200K images annotated for object detection, segmentation, and captioning tasks [N2-F2]. The official COCO page also notes that the dataset comprises 80 object categories, including common objects like cars, bicycles, animals, and more specific categories such as umbrellas, handbags, and sports equipment [N2-F2]. This broad category set makes the dataset suitable for diverse research on object-level understanding.

Annotations provided for each image include object bounding boxes, segmentation masks, and captions [N2-F2]. The COCO dataset also includes multiple annotation types for object detection, keypoint detection, and related tasks, with the official page listing features such as object segmentation, recognition in context, and superpixel information [N2-R2], [N2-R3]. The Ultralytics documentation emphasizes that the dataset provides standardized evaluation metrics like mean Average Precision (mAP) for object detection and mean Average Recall (mAR) for segmentation tasks [N2-F2]. These metrics make COCO useful for comparing model performance across implementations.

The dataset is split into three main subsets: Train2017, Val2017, and Test2017, with 118K, 5K, and 20K images respectively [N2-F2]. The train and validation splits are used for training and validation, while the test split is used for benchmarking; ground truth annotations for the test set are not publicly available, and results must be submitted to the COCO evaluation server [N2-F2]. The Ultralytics documentation also mentions that COCO is split into three subsets, and the YAML defines paths for train2017.txt, val2017.txt, and test2017.txt [N2-F2]. This split structure is important for reproducible training, evaluation, and ablation studies.

For resolution, image formats, and metadata, the evidence is thinner than the annotation and split details, but the Ultralytics documentation notes that the dataset is used for object detection, segmentation, and captioning, and that it includes detailed annotations for object segmentation [N2-F2]. The Labellerr excerpt also highlights that COCO includes detailed annotations for object segmentation and other modalities, but it does not provide exact resolution values or image-format specifics in the excerpts provided [N2-R5]. Nevertheless, the overall metadata structure is sufficient to support model training, because the dataset provides standardized paths, classes, and evaluation metrics in the YAML, and it is used with pretrained models and training pipelines such as YOLO, Faster R-CNN, and SSD [N2-F2].

In short, COCO’s key features are its large scale, 80 categories, multi-task annotations, standardized benchmark metrics, and clear train/val/test splits. These features make it a practical and widely used dataset for computer vision research [N1-F1], [N2-F2], [N2-R2].

Taken together, COCO is important for vision and language research because it is large, standardized, and multi-task: it supports object detection, segmentation, and captioning, it provides structured annotations and evaluation metrics, and it is used by computer vision and vision-language researchers for benchmarking and progress tracking [N1-F1], [N2-F2], [N1-R2].
